questions.title: Main site of heme synthesis
questions.question: The main site of heme synthesis is:

explanations.A: Correct. The bone marrow (the erythroid series) is the main site of haem synthesis, since haem is needed in huge quantity to fill the haemoglobin of every new red cell being produced. The liver is a secondary site, contributing especially to cytochrome and other haem-protein synthesis rather than to the bulk erythroid demand.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The kidney is the main adult site of erythropoietin production, not of haem synthesis itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The liver does synthesise haem, mainly for its own cytochromes, but it is a secondary site; the erythroid marrow's bulk demand for haemoglobin production makes it the main site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mature RBC has already completed haemoglobin synthesis before it loses its nucleus and mitochondria; it can no longer synthesise new haem once it enters the circulation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. White blood cells do not require haem in the way erythroid cells do, and are not a site of haem synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the bone marrow as the main site of haem synthesis, with the liver as a secondary site.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.138 (Bio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q5); same fact stated directly in the notes-format Biochemistry Notes section, p.131, item 9

questions.title: Regulatory (rate-limiting) enzyme for heme synthesis
questions.question: The regulatory enzyme for heme synthesis is:

explanations.A: Correct. ALA synthase, the mitochondrial enzyme that condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid, catalyses the first step of haem synthesis. Haem itself feeds back on this enzyme to switch production down when haem is abundant, which is what makes it the pathway's rate-limiting, regulatory step. Every later enzyme in the pathway can only act as fast as ALA synthase supplies its substrate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Haem synthase" is not a standard name for any single enzyme in this pathway; ferrochelatase (which inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX) is sometimes informally called this, but it is the final step, not the regulatory one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase acts partway through the cytosolic steps of the pathway; it is not the rate-limiting, first-step enzyme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protoporphyrinogen oxidase acts later in the mitochondrial steps, close to the pathway's end, not at its regulatory first step.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ferrochelatase catalyses the final step (inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX), not the first, rate-limiting one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ALA synthase as the rate-limiting, first-step enzyme of haem synthesis, as distinct from the other named pathway enzymes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.138 (Bio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q3); same fact stated directly in the notes-format Biochemistry Notes section, p.131, item 12 ("the key rate limiting enzyme for heme synthesis")

questions.title: Enzyme completing heme synthesis from protoporphyrin
questions.question: The synthesis of heme from protoporphyrin is catalysed by the enzyme:

explanations.A: Incorrect. ALA synthase catalyses the first step of the pathway (forming ALA from glycine and succinyl-CoA), not the final step completing haem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Ferroreductase" is not one of the named enzymes of the haem synthesis pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Ferrooxidase" is likewise not one of the named enzymes of this pathway.
explanations.D: Correct. Ferrochelatase catalyses the final step of haem synthesis, inserting ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX to complete the haem molecule. This is one of the two enzymes lead poisoning blocks (with ALA dehydratase), which is why lead poisoning, like iron deficiency, produces a microcytic anaemia — but through enzyme inhibition rather than substrate shortage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. ALA dehydratase acts early, in the cytosol, converting ALA to porphobilinogen — the second step of the pathway, not the final one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ferrochelatase as the final-step enzyme of haem synthesis, and its role as one of the two enzymes lead poisoning inhibits.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.138 (Bio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q4)

questions.title: Site of bilirubin formation
questions.question: Bilirubin is formed in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The kidney excretes water-soluble breakdown products but is not itself a site where bilirubin is formed.
explanations.B: Correct. Bilirubin is formed in three places in turn: first in the reticuloendothelial system (spleen and bone marrow, where macrophages break down haemoglobin from destroyed red cells), then further processed in the liver, and finally in the intestine, where bacteria convert it to urobilinogen. The kidney is not one of these three sites.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lungs have no role in hameoglobin breakdown or bilirubin formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle contains myoglobin, not the erythrocyte mass that generates bilirubin on breakdown, and plays no role in bilirubin formation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Adipose tissue stores triglycerides and has no role in haemoglobin breakdown or bilirubin formation.

questions.learning_objective: State the sequence of sites bilirubin passes through (reticuloendothelial system, liver, intestine), and that the kidney is not one of them.

field_notes.keySource: notes-format Biochemistry Notes section, p.137, item 62 ("Bilirubin Is formed in: Spleen & bone marrow")

questions.title: Identity of direct bilirubin
questions.question: Direct bilirubin is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is fat-soluble and albumin-bound in plasma; it is the "indirect" fraction on the van den Bergh reaction, not the "direct" one.
explanations.B: Correct. "Direct" bilirubin refers to conjugated bilirubin — bilirubin the liver has attached to glucuronic acid via glucuronyl transferase, which makes it water-soluble and able to react directly with the van den Bergh reagent without first needing an accelerant, hence the name. Its water solubility is also why conjugated bilirubin, unlike unconjugated, can appear in the urine when its plasma level rises.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Biliverdin is the green intermediate formed before bilirubin itself, from haem oxygenase's action on haem; it is not what "direct bilirubin" refers to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urobilinogen is a downstream intestinal breakdown product of bilirubin (formed by gut bacteria), not the conjugated bilirubin fraction itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Stercobilin is the further-oxidised product responsible for stool colour, downstream of urobilinogen, not the conjugated bilirubin fraction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify direct bilirubin as conjugated (glucuronidated) bilirubin, and explain why its water solubility follows from conjugation.

field_notes.keySource: notes-format Biochemistry Notes section, p.137, item 66 ("Direct bilirubin is: Conjugated bilirubin"); same fact printed with a lettered key at p.144, Bio HIS references block Q33 (biliverdin-reductase question sharing this page)

questions.title: Urobilinogen pattern in haemolytic jaundice
questions.question: In haemolytic jaundice, urine and faecal urobilinogen are typically:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decreased urobilinogen in both urine and stool is closer to the pattern in obstructive jaundice, where little or no bilirubin reaches the gut to be converted to urobilinogen at all — the opposite of haemolytic jaundice's pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haemolytic jaundice increases faecal urobilinogen too, not just urinary; the excess bilirubin delivered to the gut raises both.
explanations.C: Correct. Haemolytic jaundice increases both urine and faecal urobilinogen, because increased red cell breakdown delivers more bilirubin to the liver and gut than normal, and more of it is converted to urobilinogen by gut bacteria and reabsorbed or excreted. Faecal stercobilinogen (urobilinogen's gut-stage name) tracks how much bilirubin reaches the intestine, so it rises in haemolysis, falls in hepatocellular jaundice, and disappears in obstruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urobilinogen being absent from both urine and stool describes complete obstruction, not haemolysis, where the opposite (an excess) is seen.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Urinary urobilinogen is not absent in haemolytic jaundice; both urine and faecal urobilinogen rise together in this condition.

questions.learning_objective: State that both urine and faecal urobilinogen rise in haemolytic jaundice, as distinct from the obstructive pattern where both fall.

field_notes.keySource: notes-format Biochemistry Notes section, p.137, item 71 ("Hemolytic jaundice: increased urine urobilinogen, increased fecal urobilinogen")
